query: For Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state, the factors governing its phase stability during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure are not understood well enough to account for the range of phases that may appear. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain this behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations relative to that baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Elemental segregation during cooling induces localized elastic strains in the initially homogeneous high‐temperature BCC Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy, and these local stress fields lower the nucleation barrier for transformation to secondary phases (e.g., sigma or ordered B2 phases) during subsequent thermal exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a high‐temperature, supersaturated, single‐phase BCC structure with a nominally uniform elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Compare samples subjected to different cooling protocols: one set is slow cooled (or left untreated) to permit moderate diffusion and segregation versus a control set that is rapidly quenched or pre‐homogenized to minimize segregation. Both sets are then subjected to a defined annealing treatment (e.g., 600–900 °C for a fixed time).
generation.conditions: This mechanism is expected to dominate when the cooling rate is moderate—allowing diffusion‐mediated element partitioning (especially for elements with significantly different atomic sizes such as Cr and Al)—and when subsequent thermal exposure is in a temperature range that promotes further diffusion and elastic stress relief. It should not apply if the cooling is so rapid that segregation is suppressed or if pre‐homogenization eliminates compositional gradients before cooling.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized regions of chemical heterogeneity and lattice distortion (elastic strain fields) at nascent phase boundaries formed by differential segregation.
generation.mechanism: During cooling from the high-temperature BCC state, differences in atomic diffusivities and size mismatches (notably between the larger Cr atoms and the smaller Al atoms) lead to the onset of micro‐segregation. This segregation creates local elastic stresses that in turn lower the energy barrier for transforming to secondary phases such as sigma or ordered B2. Upon subsequent thermal exposure, these stressed regions more readily nucleate the new phases, thus explaining the range of phases observed.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples cooled under conditions that allow segregation (slow cooling without pre‐homogenization) will exhibit detectable secondary phases (e.g., sigma or B2) and altered mechanical properties (such as increased hardness from internal stresses) after annealing compared to samples that are quenched or pre‐homogenized, which should remain closer to a single BCC phase.
generation.baseline: A control alloy either rapidly quenched from the high-temperature state or pre‐homogenized to minimize compositional gradients will maintain a more uniform BCC microstructure and not exhibit the same degree of elastic internal stress or secondary phase formation during the same thermal exposure.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis should be valid when cooling rates and annealing temperatures permit moderate diffusion to trigger segregation without complete homogenization or full equilibrium; it may not apply at extreme cooling rates (e.g., melt-spinning) or at temperatures high enough to erase segregation effects by promoting complete elemental mixing.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from PMC8705824 indicates that increasing element segregation during annealing correlates with elastic stress buildup and phase transformation, and PMC7282864 shows that atomic size mismatch and lattice distortions affect transformation orientation, extending these ideas to the Cr-rich Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy is novel. The quantitative role of individual elemental diffusivities and the exact stress thresholds for phase nucleation in this particular composition remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples. Batch A receives a homogenization anneal prior to cooling and is then quenched rapidly to lock in a uniform BCC phase. Batch B is slow cooled from the high-temperature state to allow elemental segregation. Both batches are then annealed isothermally (e.g., at 700 °C for 1 hour). Subsequently, use X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (with EDS mapping) to identify the presence and distribution of any secondary phases. In parallel, perform microhardness testing to assess differences in elastic stress levels.
measurements: SEM with EDS for observing compositional segregation
Microhardness measurements to infer internal stress differences
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both Batch A (homogenized/quenced) and Batch B (slow cooled) display the same phase composition and similar mechanical properties after annealing, then the hypothesis that segregation-induced elastic stresses are driving the phase transformation would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: A detailed microstructural evaluation was executed on the crystallographic texture as well as the mechanisms for nucleation, phase transformation, and grain growth in a Al0.7CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy. The microstructure and crystallographic orientations were characterized by electron backscatter diffraction, and the chemical composition variations by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy. The cast Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy started in the BCC phase and partially transformed into the FCC phase. It was found that the Pitsch orientation relationship (OR) dominates the nucleation mechanism of the FCC phase; however, deviations with respect to the Pitsch OR are observed and are attributed to the differently sized atoms forming an ordered B2 phase in the alloy causing lattice distortions. The dual phase BCC–FCC microstructure contains FCC Widmanstätten plates oriented parallel to the {110}BCC planes of the parent grain. It was found that the crystal orientation distribution after the BCC–FCC phase transformation is confined and is explained as a product of the governing mechanisms.

AbstractIn the present study, powder of FeCoCrNiMo0.5Al1.3 HEA was manufactured by gas atomization process, and then used for laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) and microplasma spraying (MPS) technologies. The processes of phase composition and microstructure transformation during above mentioned processes and subsequent heat treatment were analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and differential thermal analysis (DTA) methods. It was found that gas atomization leads to a formation of dendrites of body centered cubic (BCC) supersaturated solid solution with insignificant Mo-rich segregations on the peripheries of the dendrites. Annealing leads to an increase of element segregations till to decomposition of the BCC solid solution and formation of σ-phase and B2 phase. Microstructure and phase composition of L-PBF sample are very similar to those of the powder. The MPS coating has a little fraction of face centered cubic (FCC) phase because of Al oxidation during spraying and formation of regions depleted in Al, in which FCC structure becomes more stable.
